title: NoteFormat
description: Shape contract for the note-formatting pass: ONE clinical note restructured into the four sections a clinician reads — why the patient is here, what they carry, what was decided, and what they take. Its input is the same single note the vital-signs pass sees; that pass pulls numbers out, this one reorganises the prose. Every item carries the span of the note it came from, so the rewriting can be checked rather than trusted.

x-notes.propertyOrder: LOAD-BEARING, and NOT the order a clinician reads. llama.cpp compiles properties into the grammar in the order given, so this is the order the model must emit them in, and `plan` is decoded BEFORE `current_medication` on purpose. Measured on a sibling pack: with medication first, the model emitted a drug on 1 of 4 notes that prescribe one — and the one that worked was the only note with no 'Plan:' heading. It partitions by the note's own headings, so a sentence under Plan reaches the plan and nothing else, and three rounds of prompt instruction did not move it. Decoding the plan first means the drug sentences are already in context, in the model's own words, when the medication list is produced: the section stops being a second reading of the note and becomes a re-reading of what was just written. PRESENTATION IS A SEPARATE CONCERN — an application renders these four in whatever order a clinician reads them, and reordering keys here reorders nothing a user sees.
x-notes.quoteBeforeText: Within an item, `quote` is emitted BEFORE `text`, which is the reverse of the vital-signs schema — where `raw_text` comes last so the quote is chosen to fit the value rather than the value to fit the quote. The tasks differ in which field is derived from which. There, `value` transcribes a number that also appears in the quote, and the danger is a citation retrofitted to a number the model already committed to. Here, `text` is an EDIT of the quote: the model strips a verb, splits a coordination. Emitting the source span first means the edit derives from something already fixed and checkable; emitting it last would let the model write the tidy version and then hunt for a span resembling it, which is how a plausible sentence that is not in the note gets evidence attached to it.
x-notes.whyBothFields: Measured on a sibling pack before this field existed: of 28 items the model emitted, 23 were the note's own words and 5 were reconstructions — and one of those five silently turned `ceftriaxona` into `ceptriaxona`. Stitching is not the defect, and forbidding it would cost the one-fact-per-item structure that makes the sections readable; the defect is stitching that cannot be checked. So the contract asks for both: the span, verifiable by literal containment, and the item, which is what a clinician reads. The derivation rule in [clinical.textDerivation] is what closes the gap between them.
x-notes.quoteIsNotCheckedBySchema: A grammar cannot constrain a string to be a substring of the prompt — no JSON Schema keyword expresses it and GBNF has no back-reference to the context. `quote` is therefore an ordinary string HERE and is verified AFTER decoding, against the rule pinned in [clinical.quoteVerification]. That split is the point: the schema guarantees the shape, the verifier guarantees the provenance, and neither pretends to do the other's job.
x-notes.arraysBounded: maxItems and uniqueItems on all three arrays, for the reason patient-summary.schema.json documents at length. CAVEAT: uniqueItems here compares whole ITEM OBJECTS, so two items differing only in `quote` are both legal — a weaker guarantee than it is over bare strings, and the prompt asks for non-repetition in addition.
x-notes.cap15: 15, below the summary's 20 and deliberately so. The summary spans a whole record; this reads ONE note, and a single note listing more than fifteen problems or fifteen plan items is not a note being formatted but a note being paraphrased line by line — which is this task's characteristic failure.
x-notes.emptyArraysAreAnswers: Every array is REQUIRED and none may be null: the one way to say a section is empty is `[]`. An empty `current_medication` is a common CORRECT answer — see the cases over the pre-assessment note and the respiratory letter, where any content at all is an invention.
x-notes.medicationIsNamesOnly: `text` in a medication item is the drug NAME alone, with amount and frequency in `dose`. Scoped this way after a measured run on a sibling pack: at whole-phrase level the model left the section empty on 3 of 4 notes that prescribe a drug, and once corrupted a drug name. A name that must be a token of a verified quote cannot drift, so that failure mode closes by construction rather than by instruction. Nothing here ENFORCES it — no keyword expresses 'a token of another property', and a maxLength would only measure the length of drug names — so the prompt asks for it and the eval measures it.
x-notes.doseIsSeparate: The dose is a third field rather than part of the name, and the split is what makes each half checkable on its own: a drug list that reads as a list of drugs, and a dose that can be compared against the note token for token. Both are verified against the same quote by the same deletion-only rule, so the strongest thing this contract says is not that the model got the dose right — it is that the model cannot state a dose the note does not contain.

presenting_complaint.description: Why the patient is here, or why the note is being written. One item rather than an array: a note has one reason for existing. null when the note does not say — never an item with an empty text, and never the diagnosis reached or the plan decided.

history.description: Problems the patient carries into this encounter: chronic, previous, or under follow-up for weeks or months. NOT the acute process that motivates this visit, not today's examination findings, and never a negation the note makes.

plan.description: What was decided: investigations requested, treatment changes, referrals, non-drug measures and follow-up. Deliberately allowed to overlap current_medication — a drug prescribed today is legitimately both, and the two items then quote the same span.

current_medication.description: DRUG NAMES ONLY in `text`, one item per drug, with amount and frequency in `dose`. A drug the note stops does not belong here; neither does oxygen, a fluid, or a diet. A drug class the note names without naming a drug ('her inhaled steroid') is not a drug name and has no item.

item.description: One fact, as the note wrote it and as the clinician should read it.

quote.description: The span of the note this item comes from, copied character by character. Verified after decoding by literal containment under [clinical.quoteVerification]; a quote that does not verify makes the item uncitable, whatever it says.

text.description: The item as it should appear in the formatted note: the quote with the sentence machinery removed. Derived from the quote, which is why it is emitted second.

medication.description: One drug: the sentence that names it, the name, and the dose that sentence gives. Its own definition rather than the shared item, because a drug is the one fact in a formatted note with a second component that must be transcribed rather than summarised.

quote.description: The span of the note this item comes from, copied character by character. Verified after decoding, exactly as an item's quote is.

text.description: The drug NAME as the note writes it, and nothing else: no dose, no schedule, no verb. Every token must be in the quote, which is what makes the name incorruptible.

dose.description: AMOUNT and FREQUENCY only, as the note writes them ('5 mg daily'), or null when the note names the drug without one ('continue her usual metformin'). It stops there on purpose: the indication ('if febrile'), the timing ('at night'), the duration and the route all belong to the plan item quoting the same sentence whole, so nothing is lost by cutting them and the field stays a column a clinician can read down. Verified against the quote by the same deletion-only rule as `text`, so a dose can be omitted but never invented or altered.
